extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, naval officers, government officials, and students of international/maritime law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of rules and principles governing maritime conduct in wartime (armed neutrality, contraband, blockades, reprisals, prize law, neutral commerce, and Orders in Council). Aimed at explaining legal standards and state practice for handling neutral trade and captures at sea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Armed Neutrality — Principle 1: Freedom of commerce with enemy ports
rubrics_metrics.description: That commerce with the ports and roads of the enemy is free to neutral powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the first of the Baltic Code of Neutrality principles (1780). Adopted by many powers; England resisted the code because it conflicted with generally acknowledged Law of Nations and existing treaties. Relevant to decisions on legality of prizes and neutral trading rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Armed Neutrality — Principle 2: Ship covers the cargo
rubrics_metrics.description: That the ship covers the cargo (i.e., 'free ships make free goods').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed in treaties between European states (e.g., Holland and France/England in the 17th century). Treated as a correlative maxim to 'enemy's ships make enemy's goods.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Armed Neutrality — Principle 3: Contraband only by treaty definition
rubrics_metrics.description: That those merchandizes only be considered as contraband which are declared to be such by treaties with the belligerent powers, or with one of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits belligerent discretion to a treaty-defined list of contraband; formed part of the Baltic Code and influenced later rules on seizure and search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Armed Neutrality — Principle 4: Blockade requires surrounding force to be effective
rubrics_metrics.description: That no place shall be considered as blockaded, till it is surrounded in such a manner by hostile ships that no person can enter it without manifest danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'effective blockade' standard used to determine legality of preventing neutral ingress/egress; appears elsewhere in the work under blockade rules and consequences of violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Armed Neutrality — Principle 5: Use as basis for prize legality
rubrics_metrics.description: That these principles shall serve as a basis for decisions concerning the legality of prizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates these neutrality principles were intended to guide prize courts' adjudications; noted that absence of British assent limited their practical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Reprisals — partial vs general reprisals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reprisals by commission, or letters of marque and reprisal, granted to injured persons in the name of the Sovereign constitute 'partial or special reprisals' and were formerly permitted in peace; general reprisals upon persons and property of subjects of another nation are equivalent to open war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains legal distinction between limited reprisals (compatible with peace historically) and broad reprisals (amounting to declaration of hostilities). Includes historical context and doubt whether old rule would hold today.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo versus reprisal — conversion by confiscation
rubrics_metrics.description: A stoppage or seizure (embargo) is preserved while hope of satisfaction exists; if hope disappears and vessels are confiscated, the embargo becomes reprisals by the act of confiscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Lord Stowell's reasoning: provisional seizure may be civil embargo if reconciliation occurs, but if hostilities follow the seizure is treated as hostile 'ab initio' and becomes subject to prize law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern rule on enemy tangible property in war
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern rule seems to be that tangible property belonging to an enemy ought not to be immediately confiscated; war gives the right to confiscate, but does not of itself confiscate the property of an enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of contemporary opinion by the author and cited authorities (e.g., Chancellor Kent). Tempering historical practice of immediate confiscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 1756 — reason 1: Identification with enemy navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Neutral vessels carrying on the previously exclusive colonial trade were considered part of the enemy navigation, 'acting in the character of French enemy' by identifying with that interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of six justifications for treating such neutral carriers as liable to capture under British practice in the 1756 controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 1756 — reason 2: Neutral carriers as enemy transports
rubrics_metrics.description: As carriers for the French, neutral vessels were to be regarded as French transports, carrying national assistance to the enemy, and therefore condemnable like vessels carrying troops or despatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported British captures of neutral ships engaged in trade that in peace was reserved to belligerents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 1756 — reason 3: Property identified with enemy interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Property carried from one part of the enemy's empire to another was so completely identified with French interests as to take a hostile character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify condemnation of neutral-carried goods moving within an enemy's empire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 1756 — reason 4: Necessity of shutting avenues of commerce in war
rubrics_metrics.description: When war comes it is necessary to shut some of the avenues of commerce, otherwise the belligerent rights could not be protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy rationale that justifies restrictions on neutral trade to protect belligerent military/economic objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 1756 — reason 5: Neutral should not gain wartime trade advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: The neutral ought not to have 'through and by means of the war' trade which he has not in time of peace; by natural justice he is only entitled to his accustomed trade, and inconveniences are balanced by enlargement of his commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that neutrals' wartime windfalls are unjust and may be curtailed to preserve belligerent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 1756 — reason 6: Neutral carriage is direct assistance to the enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a direct assistance to the enemy, and an injury to the belligerent interests of the other country, to carry on for the enemy the commerce that she has lost by the pressure of the war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final justificatory principle for condemning neutral carriers participating in previously exclusive colonial trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles declared contraband (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Items declared contraband at various times: gunpowder, arms, military equipments, sail cloths, masts, anchors, pitch, tar, hemp, cheeses fit for naval use, rosin, tallow, ship biscuits (if for naval use), certain wines, ship timber (if destined for naval use), ships of war or ships adapted for such service, copper in sheets certified fit for sheathing, brimstone (if destined to warlike port).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides illustrative list and notes that some categories (e.g., sailcloth, masts) were 'universally contraband' when destined to military ports; also notes certification (e.g., copper by dockyard officers) as a factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of a belligerent's declaration of war (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration may justify the war, waive certain belligerent rights (e.g., seizure of enemy's property on neutral vessels unless contraband), retain right to seize contraband, prevent neutrals bearing enemy despatches, maintain right to prevent breaking effective blockades, state intention not to issue letters of marque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Queen's 1854 declarations exemplify how a belligerent may selectively waive or reserve rights; such waivers do not alter the underlying international law but affect governmental exercise of belligerent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order in Council (15 April 1854) — neutral/free trade permissions
rubrics_metrics.description: All vessels under a neutral or friendly flag being neutral or friendly property shall be permitted to import into Her Majesty's dominions all goods and merchandize whatsoever and to export the same, except to blockaded ports and except those articles contraband of war or requiring special permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectively permitted broad neutral trade during hostilities (subject to blockade and contraband). The Times commentary viewed it as ending the licence system and restoring near-peacetime trade freedoms, though underlying belligerent rights remained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order in Council — limits on British vessels
rubrics_metrics.description: No British vessel shall be permitted to enter or communicate with any port or place which shall belong to or be in the possession or occupation of Her Majesty's enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where neutral trade with the enemy is allowed, British ships remained expressly forbidden from entering enemy ports, with accompanying penalties for doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjoint war and allied consent requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: During a conjoint war, no subject of an ally can trade with the common enemy without liability to forfeiture in the prize courts of the ally; this rule can be relaxed only by the permission of the allied nations according to their mutual consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Lord Stowell's broader principle that allied states should not unilaterally weaken rights that affect common operations; practical effect is that waivers of belligerent rights require allied assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraband asymmetry between belligerents
rubrics_metrics.description: Contraband to one belligerent (e.g., Russia) will not necessarily be contraband to another (e.g., England), unless it falls within specific categories (despatches, enemy forces, secret agents or spies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points to the contextual and treaty-dependent nature of contraband classification; a belligerent's orders and national policy determine what is treated as contraband for its purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of neutral property on enemy ships (limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not Her Majesty's intention to claim the confiscation of neutral property, not being contraband of war, found on board enemy's ships; neutral property on board an enemy's vessel is not generally liable to seizure, unless on an 'armed vessel of force.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows a policy preference to avoid confiscating neutral property except in circumstances (e.g., armed enemy vessels) which might justify seizure; this was reflected in proclamations and Orders in Council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Orders on licences and illegal trading doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The Order in Council of 15 April purports to end the system of licences and the doctrine of illegal trading with the enemy (as regards British practice), by conferring at once and indiscriminately the liberty to trade which licences previously granted selectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary commentary (The Times) argued this change reduced litigation and abuses associated with licences, but the Orders were a waiver of governmental action, not a change in international law; other belligerents could still restrict trade.
